items.readable_text:
Content:
Suppose that we have the arithmetic sequence
[MATH: 4, \: 7, \: 10, \: 13, \: 16, \: 19.]
The sum of all of the terms of an arithmetic sequence is known as an arithmetic series. Here, the arithmetic series for the arithmetic sequence above is
[MATH: S=4+7+10+13+16+19.]

Content:
We can write this sum more compactly using sigma notation. But first, we need to find a formula for the [MATH: n]th term in the series.

Content:
For our series above, the first term is [MATH: a_1=4] and the common difference is
[MATH: d|= a_{2} − a_{1}; = 7 − 4; = 3.]

Content:
So, the formula for the [MATH: n]th term is

Content:
[MATH: a_{n}|= a_{1} + (n − 1)d; = 4 + (n − 1)(3); = 4 + 3n − 3; = 3n + 1.]

Content:
There are [MATH: 6] terms in total, from [MATH: n={\color{black}1}] to [MATH: n={\color{red}6}.] So the sigma notation for the given series is:
[MATH: S = \sum_{n={\color{black}1}}^{\color{red}6} \left({\color{blue}3n+1}\right)]

Content:
If we expand the above series out term-by-term, we have
[MATH: S|= (3 ⋅ 1 + 1) + (3 ⋅ 2 + 1) + (3 ⋅ 3 + 1) + (3 ⋅ 4 + 1) + (3 ⋅ 5 + 1) + (3 ⋅ 6 + 1); = 4 + 7 + 10 + 13 + 16 + 19,]
which is our original sum.

Content:
Watch out! It's important to understand the difference between a sequence and a series. A sequence is a list of numbers (separated by commas). A series is what you get when you add all of the terms of a sequence together.

Since we know two terms of the arithmetic series, we can find its common difference:

[MATH: d|= (a_{9} − a_{5})/(9 − 5); = (7 − 17)/(4); = (− 10)/(4); = − (5)/(2)]

Knowing that [MATH: a_{5}=17,] we can use the formula for the [MATH: n]th term to compute [MATH: a_1,] as follows:

[MATH: a_{n}|= a_{1} + (n − 1)d; 17|= a_{1} + (5 − 1)(− (5)/(2)); 17|= a_{1} − 10; a_{1}|= 27]

So we have [MATH: a_1 = 27] and [MATH: d=-\dfrac 52.] Therefore, the formula for the [MATH: n]th term is

[MATH: a_{n}|= 27 + (n − 1)(− (5)/(2)); = 27 − (5)/(2)n + (5)/(2); = − (5)/(2)n + (59)/(2).]

Finally, the sum of the first [MATH: {\color{red}11}] terms can be written as

[MATH: ∑_(n = 1)^(11)(− (5)/(2)n + (59)/(2)).]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Suppose that we have the arithmetic sequence
[MATH: 4, \: 7, \: 10, \: 13, \: 16, \: 19.]
The sum of all of the terms of an arithmetic sequence is known as an arithmetic series. Here, the arithmetic series for the arithmetic sequence above is
[MATH: S=4+7+10+13+16+19.]

Content:
We can write this sum more compactly using sigma notation. But first, we need to find a formula for the [MATH: n]th term in the series.

Content:
For our series above, the first term is [MATH: a_1=4] and the common difference is
[MATH: d|= a_{2} − a_{1}; = 7 − 4; = 3.]

Content:
So, the formula for the [MATH: n]th term is

Content:
[MATH: a_{n}|= a_{1} + (n − 1)d; = 4 + (n − 1)(3); = 4 + 3n − 3; = 3n + 1.]

Content:
There are [MATH: 6] terms in total, from [MATH: n={\color{black}1}] to [MATH: n={\color{red}6}.] So the sigma notation for the given series is:
[MATH: S = \sum_{n={\color{black}1}}^{\color{red}6} \left({\color{blue}3n+1}\right)]

Content:
If we expand the above series out term-by-term, we have
[MATH: S|= (3 ⋅ 1 + 1) + (3 ⋅ 2 + 1) + (3 ⋅ 3 + 1) + (3 ⋅ 4 + 1) + (3 ⋅ 5 + 1) + (3 ⋅ 6 + 1); = 4 + 7 + 10 + 13 + 16 + 19,]
which is our original sum.

Content:
Watch out! It's important to understand the difference between a sequence and a series. A sequence is a list of numbers (separated by commas). A series is what you get when you add all of the terms of a sequence together.

---

So, the formula for the [MATH: n]th term is

There are [MATH: 7] terms in total, from [MATH: n={\color{black}1}] to [MATH: n={\color{red}7}.] So, the sigma notation for the given sum is
[MATH: \sum_{n={\color{black}1}}^{\color{red}7} \left({\color{blue}4n+6}\right).]
